1051-sartor-resartus-the-life-and-opinio:
Thomas Carlyle pretends to review a German book on clothes by one Diogenes Teufelsdröckh, and from that joke builds a wild philosophy. Clothes, he argues, are the outward show of all human works: laws, churches, and customs are but garments for the spirit within. The prose storms along in a mix of German fancy and Scots bluster.

Teufelsdröckh's life story, from a bleak youth to a vision of Yes after long No, gives the book its spine. Carlyle preaches work, silence, and duty against doubt and sham. The book baffled its first readers and then became a cult text, and it still rewards those who like big ideas in strange dress.
28885-alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland-i:
Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland appears here in the edition illustrated by Arthur Rackham, with a proem by Austin Dobson. Rackham's black-and-white drawings give Alice a fresh look. Dobson's verses note that forty years had passed since Carroll first sent Alice wondering through a land half comic and half tragic. The book opens with Carroll's own golden-afternoon poem about the boat trip that begged the tale into being.

Inside, Alice follows the White Rabbit, meets the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, and the Queen of Hearts, and grows and shrinks through a dream world. Rackham's pictures, famous from Rip Van Winkle, dress the familiar story in new costume. Readers get a classic text in a handsome artist's edition, suited to both first readers and collectors.

sartor-resartus-the-life-and-opinions-of:
Thomas Carlyle published Sartor Resartus in 1831, giving the book a subtitle that presents it as the life and opinions of Herr Teufelsdrockh. The opening chapter, called Preliminary, starts with a complaint. Learning has grown for five thousand years and more, Carlyle argues, yet almost no deep study in philosophy or history takes clothes as its subject.

He sharpens the point by naming fields that now look settled or complete. Astronomy can predict the planets, and earth science can explain how worlds form. Thinkers have produced accounts of rent, value, language, and much more. Clothes alone, he says, have been passed over, even though dress covers the body and shapes how a person meets the world. The rest of the book takes up that neglected subject.
